connections.why: Electron configuration determines the type of bonding and molecular shape
Relative atomic mass from isotopes is needed for mole and formula calculations
Periodic trends explain the reactivity and behaviour of the groups
Bond enthalpies link bonding to the energy changes of reactions
Covalent bonding and shape underpin organic structures and mechanisms
Balancing redox half-equations builds on amount-of-substance work
Oxidation numbers extend to electrode potentials and electrochemical cells
Variable oxidation states and redox chemistry are central to transition metals
Hess's-law enthalpy work extends to Born–Haber cycles and free energy
Qualitative kinetics develops into rate equations and reaction orders
Le Chatelier predictions are quantified through equilibrium constants Kc and Kp
Equilibrium principles are applied to pH, Ka and buffer solutions
Titration calculations require confident use of moles and concentrations
Enthalpy of hydration and stability ideas explain transition-metal behaviour
Transition metals act as catalysts studied through rate equations
Reactions of alcohols and halogenoalkanes lead into carbonyl and acid chemistry
Carbonyl and carboxylic acid chemistry builds toward arenes, amines and polymers
Organic structures are identified using mass spectrometry and infrared
Complex organic products are determined by NMR and chromatography
Reactions of group oxides connect inorganic chemistry to acid–base behaviour
Coloured complexes and their structures are probed by spectroscopic methods
